content: Kikayon (קיקיון) is the Hebrew name of a plant mentioned in the Biblical Book of Jonah. The term kikayon first appears in the Book of Jonah, specifically in Chapter 4. The word kikayon is unique to the Book of Jonah, and there is ongoing debate regarding the exact identity of the plant. Some scholars suggest it could be a gourd, while others propose it might be a castor oil plant. An alternative interpretation suggests that the description of the kikayon might refer to an entheogenic mushroom, such as the fly agaric (Amanita muscaria). Mushrooms, including Amanita muscaria, grow and wither very quickly, often within a single night, which aligns with the Biblical description. In ancient times, mushrooms were not cultivated because their spores are invisible to the naked eye, making their growth appear spontaneous. In some cultures, the Amanita muscaria mushroom is associated with and named after umbrellas or parasols due to its distinctive shape, which could correspond to the shadow over Jonah's head mentioned in the text. Interestingly, the red cap of Amanita muscaria was also symbolically linked to the sun because of its round shape and bright color. When the mushroom cap is dried, its color changes from red to gold, resembling the rising sun in the sky. The description of the rising sun mushroom cap beating down on Jonah's head and causing him to faint could be interpreted as a reference to the effects of fly agaric intoxication. In ancient times, creatures such as worms, maggots, serpents, and dragons were often grouped together under a single category. For example, the Old English word wyrm could refer to any of these beings. These creatures symbolized chthonic (underworld) forces, a category to which the Amanita muscaria mushroom was also associated. In Sanskrit, the names for mushrooms, such as ahichattraka and sarpacchattraka, translate to snake parasol, further emphasizing the symbolic connection between mushrooms and serpentine or chthonic imagery.
